newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland army base bombed, two critically hurt.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland army base bombed, two critically hurt.

text.p: Suspected Irish Republican guerrillas bombed Britain's army headquarters in Northern Ireland on Monday, injuring up to 20 people, two critically, and shattering an uneasy two-year peace in the province.
Military and civilian hospitals said around 20 people were being treated, including an eight-year-old girl, and the condition of two, who were not identified, was grave.

Police and army said what appeared to be a car bomb exploded in a car park inside Britain's Northern Ireland army nerve centre, while a second appeared to have been placed to hit people being evacuated to an army medical centre for treatment.
British Prime Minister John Major, the target of Irish Republican criticism for his handling of a two-year peace process, said the attack was "wicked beyond belief."

"To have placed a bomb without warning to kill or maim innocent men and women and then to place a second bomb where those people already injured and maimed might be caught as they sought medical attention, or to kill the people giving them medical attention, is just unspeakable," he said.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack but Protestant pro-British spokesman blamed Irish Republicans fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
"This is clearly the work of Republicans," said David Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, the main mouthpiece of a 60 percent pro-British Protestant majority.
It was the first guerrilla attack on a British security target since rival Irish Republican Army (IRA) and Protestant Loyalist guerrillas declared twin ceasefires in 1994.

The IRA ended its 17-month truce in February but has limited attacks to the British mainland. The barracks bomb raised fears that the Loyalists would now restart attacks against the Catholic community from which the Irish Republican movement draws support.
Police fear that any IRA attack in the province itself would unleash a Loyalist backlash which could spread to the Irish Republic. Loyalists accuse of the Dublin government of backing the IRA.

Speaking to BBC television from a conference in the United States, British Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew said: "This attack will do nothing but bring catastrophe if Loyalist paramilitaries go back to violence and I appeal to them to hold to their discipline."

Army sources were baffled at how any group could penetrate the top-security Thiepval barracks, which houses hundreds of Britain's senior soldiers and thousands of troops and families in an 18,000-strong force.

Reverend Brian Gibson, who lives next door to the barracks, said: "I was sitting in my study when it went off. I could see shrapnel all over the playing field. It seemed to be in the middle of a field where some girls were playing hockey.
"There was no screaming, just an awful silence for a considerable length of time. Then all the emergency services started to arrive," he said.
The attack was mounted as jailed Loyalists in the top-security Maze prison met to discuss whether or not their activists should continue to abide by an October 1994 ceasefire.
The blasts could be heard at the prison where 1,000 people, both Republican and Loyalist, are detained for security offences in the 27-year Northern Ireland conflict.
The explosions came on the eve of this week's conference of Major's ruling Conservative Party.

Irish Republicans accuse the prime minister of wrecking the peace process by insisting that the IRA end its violence before its political wing, Sinn Fein, can be admitted to multi-party talks on Northern Ireland's political future.
